topics.description: Gold is the chemical element with atomic number 79 and symbol Au, a dense, lustrous, highly malleable yellow precious metal.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Frederick Hodgson’s attempt to acquire an object made from this substance sparked a war with Queen Yaa Asantewaa. That object is this substance’s “stool." The price of this substance in Mamluk Egypt deflated after Mansa Musa’s hajj. The trade of (*) salt and this substance in the trans-Saharan trade made West African empires, like Mali, prosperous. For 10 points, name this valuable metal, which sparked many “rushes” throughout history.
parts.answer: gold [accept Golden Stool before “stool” is read; or gold rushes]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The Kingdom of Mapungubwe controlled the trade of ivory and this resource in southern Africa until it was overtaken by the Kingdom of Zimbabwe. The ancient Egyptian word for this resource, nbw (“na-baw”), may be the source of the name of Nubia, which contained much of it. Camel caravans brought a different resource from sites like Taghaza to trade for this resource in cities like (*) Djenne. The market for this resource in Cairo crashed when Mansa Musa brought copious amounts of it with him on his hajj. The Trans-Saharan trade route for salt and this resource was fought over by empires like Songhai, Ghana, and Mali. For 10 points, name this precious metal with a yellow color.

topics.description: A speculative bubble in the Dutch tulip market during the 1630s, when tulip bulb prices rose dramatically before collapsing.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: It’s not Japan, but the term rangaku refers to technology acquired from this country through the port of Dejima. Charles Mackay described a “mania” in this country where the price of tulips spiked, then plunged. This non-British country founded Batavia in its (*) “East Indies,” which consisted of colonies in what is now modern-day Indonesia. For 10 points, name this country ruled by the House of Orange, which is the namesake of Dutch disease.
parts.answer: the Netherlands [or Holland; or the Kingdom of the Netherlands; or Koninkrijk der Nederlanden]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The decline of this country’s industrial sector in the mid-18th century is derisively known as the “Periwig Era.” This country’s colonial ventures were overseen by companies operated by the 19 Gentlemen and 17 Gentlemen. This country’s financial innovations included hosting the first publicly traded company and the first (*) stock exchange. This country expanded its farmland and created a vast system of polders using windmills. In the 1630s, a speculative bubble drove up the price of tulips in this country, then collapsed dramatically. For 10 points, name this European country whose stock exchange was hosted in Amsterdam.
parts.answer: The Netherlands [or Kingdom of the Netherlands or Nederland or Koninkrijk Nederlanden accept Dutch Republic or Republic of the Seven United Netherlands or United Provinces of the Netherlands]

topics.description: The transcontinental country spanning Eastern Europe and northern Asia, formally known as the Russian Federation.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Leon Trotsky negotiated the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk to pull this country out of World War I. For ten points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this country that was in the midst of overthrowing its monarchy in St. Petersburg when the treaty was signed. The Mensheviks and Bolsheviks fought for control of this country throughout 1917.

parts.label: B
parts.question: This man led the Bolsheviks in the Russian Revolution and became the first leader of the USSR. St. Petersburg would be renamed after him upon his death.
parts.answer: Vladimir Lenin [accept Valdimir Ilyich Ulyanov; accept Leningrad]

parts.label: C
parts.question: This last Tsar of Russia and ruling member of the house of Romanov was overthrown in the Russian Revolution. He was murdered along with his entire family in 1918 by Bolsheviks in the Ipatiev House of Yekaterinburg.
parts.answer: Nicholas II [prompt on Nicholas or Nikolai]

topics.description: A decisive World War II battle in which Soviet forces encircled and defeated the German 6th Army at Stalingrad.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A sniper from this country, Simo Häyhä, gained the nickname “White Death” for killing hundreds of Soviet troops without using a scope during the Winter War. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Name this country whose fallen soldiers are often buried in the Hietaniemi Cemetery in Helsinki.
parts.answer: ANSWER: Finland [or Republic of Findland or Suomen tasavalta or Republiken Finland or Suomi]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Serbian snipers positioned themselves on this city’s “Sniper Alley” during the Bosnian War. A wrong turn may have led to Archduke Franz Ferdinand’s assassination in this city.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] The sniper Vasily Zaitsev killed 225 enemy soldiers during this battle. The leader of the 6th Army, Friedrich Paulus, surrendered at this battle after being encircled by Operation Uranus.

topics.description: The historical name of the Russian city now called Volgograd, especially associated with the Battle of Stalingrad.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The song of this river’s boatmen was arranged for orchestra by Igor Stravinsky. For ten points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this longest river in Europe, whose canal to the Don River helps ultimately connect cities like Kazan and Nizhny Novgorod to the ocean.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Vologorad, a city on the Volga River, was previously known by this name. The massive Motherland Calls statue commemorates the five-month-long World War II siege of Volgograd under this name.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Volgograd now lies in this country, the largest successor of the USSR.
parts.answer: Russia [or Russian Federation or Rossiyskaya Federatsiya or Rossiya]

topics.description: A campaign of state terrorism and forced disappearance conducted by Argentina’s military dictatorship, chiefly from 1976 to 1983, against suspected political opponents.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: In an event celebrated on “Loyalty Day,” supporters of a leader of this country chanted “alpargatas yes, books no,” in reference to the shoes worn by this country’s poor. In 1947, the first lady of this country visited many European countries during her goodwill “Rainbow Tour.” Working-class supporters of that woman’s husband were called the (*) “Shirtless Ones,” or descamisados. The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo gather on Thursdays to protest the children who disappeared during this country’s Dirty War. This country fought the United Kingdom in a brief war for control of the Falkland Islands. For 10 points, name this country once led by Juan Perón with capital at Buenos Aires.
parts.answer: Argentina [or Argentine Republic or República Argentina]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: A revolutionary born in this country had his photo taken after the La Coubre explosion by Alberto Korda.  This country’s descamisados were bombed in its Plaza de Mayo in 1955. A regime in this country waged the  (*) “Dirty War” against its political opponents under Jorge Videla, and later went to war with Britain over the  Falkland Islands. For 10 points, name this country led by Juan Peron from a pink palace in Buenos Aires.
parts.answer: Argentina [or Argentine Republic; or Republica Argentina]

topics.description: A scholarly and translation institution in Abbasid Baghdad associated with preserving and translating Greek, Persian, and Indian works.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Callimachus’ lost work Pinakes [PIN-ah-keez] listed the contents of one of these locations. Legend says that, after Hulagu Khan’s 1258 siege of Baghdad, the Tigris River turned black because of the destruction of one of these places, the House of (*) Wisdom. Alexandria contained a “Great” one of, for ten points, what educational facilities that stored tablets, papyrus scrolls, or other scholarly writings?

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The Palace of the Golden Gate was at the center of this city’s original “Round” design. This city’s Nahrawan Canal was destroyed by Turkish ghulams revolting with the Buyid dynasty. The Barmakid family financed the Translation Movement of Greek Texts in this city at an institution rumored to serve as a (*) library for Al-Mansur. The last ruler of a dynasty based in this city was wrapped in a carpet and trampled by the horses of Hulegu Khan. Harun al-Rashid established the House of Wisdom in this city. For 10 points, name this capital of the Abbasid Caliphate during the Islamic Golden Age that now serves as the capital of Iraq.

topics.description: A modern Jewish nationalist movement advocating the establishment and support of a Jewish homeland in the historic Land of Israel.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The Balfour Declaration supported the creation of a “national home” for members of a certain religion, which became this country. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this country that was invaded by five Arab nations shortly after its creation in 1948.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Theordor Herzl founded this movement in the late 19th Century to advocate for the establishment of a Jewish homeland. This movement was named after a word in the Bible that referred to the Land of Israel as a whole.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] The land that became Israel was a territory with this name. A territory with this name claims Gaza and the West Bank in an ongoing conflict with Israel.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Followers of this religion in the Banu Qurayza tribe were defeated at the Battle of the Trench. The “Beta” community of this religious group in Ethiopia were airlifted to an Asian country in Operation Solomon. Members of this religion descended from Middle Eastern groups are known as Mizrahi. Aliyah is the primary tenet of a movement involving this religious group, Zionism. For 10 points, name this target of anti-Semitism that populates much of Israel.

topics.description: A landlocked Central European country occupying much of the Carpathian Basin, with Budapest as its capital and a history encompassing the medieval Hungarian kingdom, the Austro-Hungarian Empire, the Holocaust, and the 1956 revolution.

parts.label: L
parts.question: A leader of this country used the term “salami tactics” to describe the method by which the Smallholders’ Party and other enemies were defeated. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this country. Mátyás Rákosi (“MAH-tahsh RAH-koh-shee”) was ousted three months before the beginning of an anti-Soviet revolution which saw Imre Nagy (“Nahj”) rise to power in this country.
parts.answer: Hungary [or Magyarország; accept Hungarian People's Republic or Magyar Népköztársaság]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Rákosi’s position in Hungary faltered after this 1956 address denouncing Joseph Stalin was delivered at the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.
parts.answer: Khrushchev’s Secret Speech [or “On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences”]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] After Nagy replaced Rákosi as Prime Minister, Hungary briefly withdrew from the Pact named for this city, the capital of Poland.
parts.answer: Warsaw [or Capital City of Warsaw or Warszawa]

parts.label: L
parts.question: A woman born in this country was a Jewish paratrooper who was executed by the Nazis for attempting to rescue Jews from Yugoslavia. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this home country of Hannah Senesh. Thousands of Jews in this country were saved after being given Swedish passports by Raoul Wallenberg.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Senesh attempted to save Jews en route to this place, which contained iron gates with the phrase “arbeit macht frei” (AR-bait mokt FRAI).

parts.label: C
parts.question: Senesh and fellow Hungarian Rudolf Kastner assisted Jews during this genocide of six million Jews by the Nazis.

topics.description: An Indigenous people of south-central Chile and western Argentina, historically resistant to Spanish and later Chilean and Argentine expansion and involved in ongoing territorial disputes.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This country's politics were once dominated by the “Generation of '80,” including Julio Roca,  who earlier displaced the Mapuche (mah-POO-chay) people during this country's Conquest of the  Desert. The 25th article of this country's 1853 constitution promoted European immigration,  leading to 60% of this country's present-day population having (*) Italian ancestry. The 1881  Boundary Treaty divided Tierra del Fuego (tee-AIR-ah del FWAY-goh) between this country and a  smaller neighbor that shares Patagonia. For 10 points, name this country that has a 3300-mile long  border with Chile.
parts.answer: Argentina [or Argentine Republic; or Republica Argentina]

parts.label: L
parts.question: For 10 points each, answer the following about colonial explorers who met violent ends:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] This Spanish explorer was put on trial and beheaded in Panama by a rival colonial administrator. Earlier, he was the first European to cross the Isthmus of Panama and lay eyes on the eastern shore of the Pacific Ocean.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] The conquistador Francisco Pizarro, who conquered this empire, was killed in a violent attack orchestrated by Diego de Almagro II. Pizarro himself had this Andean empire’s ruler Atahualpa executed in 1533.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] Pedro de Valdivia, the first royal governor of Chile, was killed by these indigenous people. Conflicts between Chile and this indigenous people of the Araucanía region over logging and water use are still ongoing.
